questions.q: What are the three major sources of law identified in modern legal systems according to the NCERT textbook?
questions.a: The three major sources are Custom, Judicial Precedent, and Legislation. A wrong answer (e.g., "Constitution, Parliament, Courts") reveals confusion between sources of law and organs of government — the student is mixing Chapter 8 (Sources) with Unit 1 (Political Institutions).

questions.q: Explain why a custom must satisfy the test of "reasonableness" to be recognized as law, using the Bombay High Court example from the textbook.
questions.a: A custom must conform to norms of justice and public utility; if it causes more mischief than convenience, it fails. In Mathura Naikon v. Esu Naekin (1880), the custom of adopting girls for immoral purposes was declared invalid as unreasonable and immoral. A wrong answer focusing only on "antiquity" reveals the student memorized the list of tests but doesn't understand they work together — a 500-year-old custom can still be invalid if unreasonable.

questions.q: The Supreme Court in 2015 banned diesel cars registered before 2005 in Delhi NCR. The judgment included remarks on construction dust and crop burning as pollution sources. A district court in Delhi is hearing a similar case in 2024. Which part of the 2015 judgment is binding on this district court, and why?
questions.a: Only the ratio decidendi (the ban on pre-2005 diesel cars based on engine deterioration and pollution) is binding. The remarks on construction dust and crop burning are obiter dicta — persuasive but not binding. A wrong answer saying "the whole judgment is binding" shows failure to distinguish ratio from obiter, a critical skill for legal reasoning.

questions.q: Compare the hierarchy of judicial precedent in India with the UK before 2009. What key structural difference explains why the UK moved to a separate Supreme Court?
questions.a: In India, the Supreme Court is separate from Parliament and the executive. In pre-2009 UK, Law Lords sat in the House of Lords (legislature) while serving as the highest court — violating separation of powers. The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 created the UK Supreme Court to fix this fusion. A wrong answer focusing only on "both have Supreme Courts" misses the constitutional principle: India's basic structure doctrine (Keshavananda Bharati) requires judicial independence as a basic feature, which the UK achieved only in 2009.

questions.q: "Delegated legislation is a necessary evil." Evaluate this statement with reference to the reasons for its growth and the safeguards in the Indian system.
questions.a: It is "necessary" because Parliament lacks time, technical expertise, and flexibility for detailed rules (e.g., traffic regulations, drug standards). It is "evil" because it transfers law-making to the unelected executive, risking arbitrariness. Safeguards: parent Act must lay down policy (delegatus non potest delegare), judicial review for ultra vires, and parliamentary oversight (laying on table). A one-sided answer ("it's good" or "it's bad") fails to evaluate — the student must weigh both sides using the textbook's "paucity of time, technicalities, emergency" vs "increasing tendency criticized."

questions.q: Create a scenario where a local custom conflicts with a central legislation. Explain which prevails and why, using the "Status of Custom with regard to Legislation" principle.
questions.a: Scenario: A tribal community in Chhattisgarh follows a custom of marrying girls at 16. The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 sets 18 as minimum age. The legislation prevails because modern law abrogates contrary customs (textbook: "when a new legislation is enacted, it is generally preferred to the custom"). A poor answer ignores the hierarchy (legislation > custom) or suggests the custom survives due to "antiquity" — showing the student hasn't grasped that validity tests include consistency with statute.
